rows.prompt: Explain the relationship between faith and reason.
rows.text:
Whether faith and reason are opposed to one another, and if not, how they relate.

Objection 1. It seems that faith and reason are opposed, for the Apostle commands us to 'test all things' (1 Thess. 5:21), which would seem to require reason, not faith. If faith were superior, it would render reason superfluous.

Objection 2. Furthermore, the Catechism teaches that faith is a 'rational acceptance' of God's self-revelation. If faith is rational, it appears to be identical with reason, not opposed to it.

On the contrary, the same Catechism, in its treatment of the Ten Commandments, affirms that faith is the 'foundation and ultimate goal of the commandments' (CCC §209), indicating that faith and reason are not rivals but rather that reason is ordered toward faith.

I answer that, faith and reason are not enemies but are rather two distinct ways of knowing the same truth, namely, the truth of God's existence and of His revelation.

The proper object of the will is the matter in respect to which the will is exercised — that is, the thing or things that are the subject of the disposition made by the testator.

Furthermore, the object must be real and certain — that is, it must be a thing that actually exists and can be clearly identified. A mere idea or a future thing not yet in existence does not suffice as an object of disposition.
